buildSteps.title: Pick a falsifiable observable
buildSteps.detail: Choose a quantity that competing quantum-gravity models predict differently — for example an energy-dependent speed of light, a loss of quantum coherence, or a minimum measurable length.

buildSteps.title: Estimate the size of the effect
buildSteps.detail: If a model predicts a deviation of one part in 10^30, no current instrument can see it, so the experiment is not yet worth building.

buildSteps.title: Design the instrument around a null test
buildSteps.detail: Compare two paths — two interferometer arms, two clocks at different heights, two polarisations — so that everything except the hypothesised effect cancels.

buildSteps.title: Suppress known noise
buildSteps.detail: Isolate from seismic, thermal, electromagnetic and gravity-gradient disturbance using vacuum, cryogenics and multi-layer suspension; otherwise the tiny signal is buried.

buildSteps.title: Reach quantum-limited sensitivity
buildSteps.detail: Use squeezed light, cold atoms or long coherence times so that measurement noise itself is not the limit.

buildSteps.title: Run for long enough
buildSteps.detail: Integrate for months or years, because the signal is a small systematic offset rather than a flash.

buildSteps.title: Cross-check against nature's accelerators
buildSteps.detail: Search the same signature in gamma rays, neutrinos and gravitational waves that have crossed the universe, where any cumulative effect is amplified by distance.

buildSteps.title: Confirm and scale
buildSteps.detail: If an anomaly survives every systematic check, replicate it on a larger baseline or a quieter site — that is how a new theory of space-time would begin.

prerequisites.why: gravitational-wave detectors already measure mirror displacements thousands of times smaller than an atomic nucleus.
free-fall times of a second or more are needed, which requires tall vacuum towers or space.
they can detect a clock ticking differently because it sits one centimetre higher in Earth's gravity.
tests of whether gravity can entangle two masses need objects heavy enough to feel gravity yet coherent enough to stay quantum.
most candidate theories are not yet precise enough to say what a given experiment should measure.

pathway.milestone: gravitational-wave detectors and clock networks set ever tighter limits on Lorentz violation, extra forces and drift of fundamental constants
pathway.unlocks: a growing list of ruled-out models rather than a positive detection.

pathway.milestone: 100-metre-scale atom interferometers such as those under construction at Fermilab and in the UK
pathway.unlocks: sensitivity to ultralight dark matter and new long-range forces, with quantum-gravity reach beyond that.

pathway.milestone: a space-based gravitational-wave observatory planned for the 2030s, plus tabletop tests of gravity-induced entanglement between two masses
pathway.unlocks: probes of space-time behaviour that no ground instrument can reach.

pathway.milestone: space-based atom interferometry and clock comparisons at Planck-scale sensitivity
pathway.unlocks: either the first observational hint of quantum gravity, or firm proof that space-time is smooth far below any accessible scale.
